newsitem.title: UK: British ministers deny rift over EMU.
newsitem.headline: British ministers deny rift over EMU.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke denied on Thursday there was a cabinet rift over Britain's position on the planned European single currency.
In response to a question from Reuters, the two men issued a statement saying government policy on European Monetary Union (EMU) remained unchanged.
"We are hostile to the notion that a single currency can proceed at any stage on a non-convergent basis," the ministers said.
"Government policy has not changed," they added.

The government had established an uneasy truce on EMU at a cabinet meeting on January 23 when it declared that while Britain would keep its options open, it was unlikely to join up if the single currency went ahead as planned in 1999.
Clarke and Rifkind said they remained committed to the statement made after that meeting.
On Wednesday, in what appeared to be a shift from the neutral policy agreed in January, Rifkind said Britain was "on balance hostile" to EMU.
Clarke said his colleague must have made "a slip of the tongue", but Rifkind retorted that he had meant what he said.
Their joint statement, issued in the early hours of Thursday, indicated they were hostile to joining EMU if European Union economies had not converged.
The Conservative government's opponents seized with glee on Wednesday's exchange between Rifkind and Clarke.
"You have got government ministers at sixes and sevens...it is a quite extraordinary situation," said opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair.
"The government can't sustain a position on Europe for a week," said Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, Britain's most pro-European party.
Rifkind made his remarks in Bonn ahead of a speech on Britain's attitude to the EU in which he emphasised the need to guard against centralisation of power to Brussels.

The single currency is a tricky issue for Prime Minister John Major because of the conflict within his party between ministers like Clarke who believe Britain should join provided it is properly set up and members of parliament who are completely opposed to it and distrust anything that emanates from Brussels.
Major must call a general election by May and with his party lagging behind Labour by around 20 points in opinion polls, he faces a struggle to regain power.
In an interview published in Thursday's Times newspaper, Clarke said Britain would be making a "terrible mistake" if it decided now to opt out of a single currency.
By doing that it "would be ruling out the possibility of making a judgment that could have a vital effect on jobs and prosperity some time in the future", he said.
But Clarke believed the planned 1999 starting date for EMU would have to be put back.
Meanwhile, Labour's pro-European shadow finance minister Gordon Brown launched into the debate from Washington, announcing he had set his own criteria for signing Britain up to a single currency.
Brown told the Financial Times there were "current obstacles" to joining the planned single European currency.
"Getting it (EMU membership) right is more important than getting it quickly," said Brown.
